commentary.bottom_line: Nine offline studies suggest that structured evaluation can detect and help raise empathy and tone scores in AI-generated patient communications, but none measured whether this evaluation changes patient harm or outcomes in real use. Hazard studies show that warmth can coexist with unsafe or therapeutically inappropriate content, so evaluations that score empathy alone may miss failures tied to clinical risk.

perspectives.view: All nine tests are level 4 and offline or simulated. Only one is randomized, with 300 patients rating texts. Outcomes are rater or model scores of empathy, tone, and clarity rather than patient outcomes. Findings point the same way, but they use different instruments and small samples, and three report no numbers. Indirectness and imprecision lower certainty.

Single-objective tuning reached 93.6% empathy but 47.8% safety in one study. In another, surface acknowledgment scored about 0.91 to 1.00 while therapeutic appropriateness fell to 0.22 to 0.33 at the highest severity. Lay raters detected 60% of expert-confirmed instances of the Endorse response style. These results suggest evaluations may need expert review of appropriateness by risk level.

An AI grader agreed with reference grades at κ=0.44, close to lay raters at κ=0.43. Distribution decisions based on AI grades matched reference decisions 88.1% of the time. Automated screening may make routine tone evaluation feasible, though agreement was moderate. In one live deployment, patients preferred human replies for tone 68% of the time over initial-prompt AI drafts.

Two tests involved non-English communication, one with Chinese-language consultations and one with 60 radiology impressions translated to Spanish. In a hazard trial that included low-literacy, low-income, and rural patients, a model tuned on local data reproduced an unfriendly clinician-like tone. This finding suggests evaluation criteria may need to reflect the intended population rather than local clinician habits.

commentary.research_gap: No study tested whether evaluating communications before or during deployment reduces patient harm, distress, or disengagement in real clinical use. Prospective studies should pair empathy and tone scoring with safety and therapeutic-appropriateness outcomes stratified by risk level. They should also validate automated graders against expert judgment and enroll low-literacy and limited English proficiency patients.
commentary.underserved_note: Two tests included non-English communication, one with Chinese-language consultations and one with 60 Spanish-translated radiology impressions. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Evaluation methods and thresholds therefore remain unvalidated for patients whose literacy and trust needs may differ most from those of the raters who set the scores.
